text:
Repeat consumption is legitimate behavior, but aggregate accuracy can conceal reliance on it. [RepeatNet](https://arxiv.org/abs/1812.02646) explicitly distinguishes repeat from explore recommendations. [Li et al., SIGIR 2023](https://staff.fnwi.uva.nl/m.derijke/wp-content/papercite-data/pdf/li-2023-repetition.pdf) find unequal difficulty between these cases, repeat samples acting as shortcuts, and shared input/output embeddings potentially favoring repetition. Thus, correctly ranking a training positive already present in its prefix does not establish generalization; neither does ranking an absent-prefix positive that was used during fitting.

Recommended diagnostic design: evaluate only valid training positions using their strictly preceding causal prefixes. For shifted sequence batches, determine target occurrence within sequence[:t+1], never the whole input row, whose later positions may contain the target. Stratify by target occurrence (absent/present; optionally count and recency), target frequency computed exclusively from training interactions (fixed tail/middle/head bins), and actual nonpadding input length (fixed short/medium/long bins). Report counts, HR@10, MRR and positive–negative score margins per category and crossed strata; mark empty or small cells. Freeze diagnostic examples, candidate sampling, exclusions and tie handling across checkpoints. These are proposed controls, not a published universal protocol. Repeat/head/long-history advantages suggest possible shortcuts, but cannot alone prove memorization; absent-prefix accuracy remains training fit.

Keep diagnostics separate from the unchanged host validation: four-category macro HR@10, 200 users/category, 99 unique negatives, seed 42. Label training results explicitly as diagnostic, never held-out performance. Candidate protocols matter: [Dallmann et al.](https://arxiv.org/abs/2107.13045) show sampled evaluation can reorder models relative to full-catalog ranking. Do not replace the fixed evaluator, alter splits, or infer full-catalog generalization from diagnostic or sampled-validation scores.
